paper_title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to strong generalization across diverse natural language processing tasks [Achiam et al., 2023, Yang et al., 2025]. To extend beyond conventional language modeling, LLM-powered agents [Luo et al., 2025] integrate action modules with controlled API access, enabling the invocation of task-specific tools and interaction with external environments [Schick et al., 2023]. This agentic design allows LLMs to address more demanding realworld challenges, including web-based information retrieval [Liu et al., 2025], software engineering [Yang et al., 2024], and scientific report generation [Li et al., 2025, OpenAI, 2025a]. In these complex settings, LLM agents typically employ iterative ReasonActObserve cycles to incrementally make progress and refine solutions [Yao et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2024]. While agents built on large proprietary backbones such as GPT-4.1 [OpenAI, 2025b] achieve high task success rates, their prohibitive token consumption and inference latency pose significant barriers to practical deployment. To bridge this efficiency gap, transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) has emerged as compelling research direction. Inspired by the success of chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation [Ho et al., 2023, Shridhar et al., 2023], recent agent distillation framework [Kang et al., 2025] leverages expert trajectories composed of (Thought, Action, Observation) tuples generated by high-capacity teachers during problem solving. By performing behavioral Correspondence to: Yuanpu Cao <yuanpu.cao@psu.edu> and Jinghui Chen <jzc5917@psu.edu>. Code is available at https://github.com/CaoYuanpu/ProD. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). cloning via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on these trajectories, SLMs are trained to emulate teacher behaviors and thereby acquire tool-augmented reasoning capabilities. However, despite familiarizing SLMs with agent execution workflows, this SFT-based distillation strategy suffers from critical limitation during task execution. Specifically, as agents perform successive ReasonActObserve iterations, the runtime context accumulates long reasoning-action chains alongside large volumes of environment-derived feedback, such as noisy web search results and code execution logs. Under these increasingly complex contexts, distilled SLM agents frequently exhibit pronounced form of progress stagnation: they become trapped in unproductive loops, persistently attempting failed strategies and actions from prior turns, and struggle to break these cycles to make forward progress. Our systematic analysis (in Section 2) reveals that this stagnation is pervasive across diverse model families (e.g., Qwen3 [Yang et al., 2025], Llama3 [Grattafiori et al., 2024], and Gemma3 [Team et al., 2025]), various task domains, and different fine-tuning paradigms. Moreover, the issue becomes increasingly severe as model scale decreases and trajectory length increases, ultimately creating fundamental bottleneck for effective agent distillation. To address this limitation, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), novel framework that explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories during the distillation process. To achieve precise intervention, ProD encodes the stagnation gap (i.e., the difference in stagnation levels) between student and teacher trajectories into an adaptive margin. This margin dynamically modulates the optimization strength, enabling aggressive correction of stagnant behaviors while preventing overcorrection on student trajectories that already closely align with teacher progress. By iteratively applying this optimization procedure, ProD substantially alleviates progress stagnation in SLM-based agents, enabling them to steadily converge toward the coherent problem-solving behaviors of high-capacity teacher agents. We summarize our contributions as follows. We identify and systematically analyze progress stagnation, pervasive failure mode in SFTbased agent distillation where SLMs collapse into unproductive loops during multi-turn interactions. Our analysis reveals that this phenomenon consistently occurs across various model families and task domains. We propose the Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD) framework, which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation exhibited in student-generated trajectories during optimization. By encoding studentteacher stagnation gap into an adaptive optimization margin, ProD dynamically penalizes possible stagnation during the distillation process. Comprehensive experiments on 8 SLMs ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both task success rates and completion efficiency for distilled SLM agents.

sections.title: 2 Progress Stagnation Analysis
sections.content: We organize this section as follows. In Section 2.1, we review the standard SFT-based agent distillation framework. In Section 2.2, we analyze the progress stagnation phenomenon in SFT-distilled SLM agents and introduce stagnation scores to quantify the associated failure modes. 2.1 Preliminaries: Agent Distillation via SFT The goal of agent distillation is to transfer agentic capabilities from powerful teacher model pT to compact student model pθ S. Under multi-turn interaction frameworks such as ReAct [Yao et al., 2023] and CodeAct [Wang et al., 2024], agent distillation typically begins by collecting execution trajectories from the teacher model. Each trajectory τ is sequence of interaction tuples consisting of thoughts (h), actions (a), and environmental observations (o). Specifically, given user query and an agent instruction agent (e.g., To solve the task, you must plan forward to proceed in series of steps, in cycle of Thought, Code, and Observation sequences. At each turn i, the agent generates reasoning thought hi and an action ai to invoke external tools. As the interaction context grows with extensive reasoning chains and environmental feedback, such as noisy search results and verbose code-execution logs, these agents frequently lapse into unproductive reasoning-action loops. In these scenarios, the student model tends to redundantly recycle ineffective strategies rather than synthesize feedback to generate novel solution directions, thereby impeding task progress. As illustrated in Figure 1 (right), an SFT-distilled agent tasked with factual reasoning query repeatedly issues highly similar web-search actions across multiple turns, despite prior attempts failing to retrieve the requisite information. This persistent failure to adapt eventually leads to task expiration or incorrect termination. In contrast, the teacher agent maintains steady progress (Figure 1, left): by effectively leveraging prior interactions, the teacher adaptively refines its actions, progressively acquiring new information until the task is successfully resolved. Stagnation Evaluation. Equipped with the proposed stagnation metric, we conduct comprehensive analysis under the CodeAct framework across diverse agentic tasks. Following the SFT distillation procedure in Section 2.1, we employ GPT-4.1 as the teacher agent to collect 3,000 trajectories from the training sets of MATH [Hendrycks et al., 2021] and HotpotQA [Yang et al., 2018], respectively. With appropriate tool set configurations [Kang et al., 2025], these benchmarks facilitate the evaluation of diverse agentic capabilities, including code-assisted numerical computation, software package execution, and web information seeking. We then distill these capabilities into various SLMs using LoRA [Hu et al., 2022], with training details provided in Appendix B.1. Figure 2 (1&2) presents turn-level lexical stagnation scores for distilled Qwen3-4B/1.7B/0.6B on held-out evaluation sets, while Figure 2 (3&4) report the average semantic and judgment stagnation across turns and datasets. The results reveal consistent pattern: distilled SLMs exhibit substantially more severe stagnation than the teacher agent, and this disparity becomes increasingly pronounced as model scale decreases or trajectory length increases. In particular, the lexical stagnation score can reach values close to 0.9, indicating that the student actions highly resemble their previous attempts. We further compute pairwise Pearson correlations among the three stagnation metrics in Table 2, finding consistently high agreement with > 0.92. This strong correlation suggests that, under severe stagnation, the three metrics capture the same underlying failure mode in SLM agents. We observe the similar stagnation trend across additional model families, including Llama3 and Gemma3 (see Section 4.2 and Appendix G). The pattern also persists under full-parameter fine-tuning, as detailed in Appendix C, and remains evident even when evaluating on the distillation training data itself (Appendix D). These findings collectively demonstrate that SFT distillation alone is insufficient for enabling SLMs to acquire the teachers resilience to stagnation.

sections.title: 3 Progress-Aware Distillation for SLM Agents

Motivated by this gap, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), training strategy that explicitly detects stagnation in student-generated trajectories and applies adaptive penalties during 4 optimization. By discouraging unproductive reasoning-action patterns, ProD enables SLM agents to maintain forward progress and more closely align with the teachers problem-solving dynamics. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Settings Student Backbones and Teacher Agent. To evaluate the effectiveness of ProD across various model scales, we select eight SLMs ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters as student backbones. Specifically, our evaluation includes the Qwen3 series (4B, 1.7B, 0.6B) [Yang et al., 2025], Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [Grattafiori et al., 2024], Llama-3.2 (3B, 1B-Instruct) [Grattafiori et al., 2024], and Gemma-3 (4B, 1B-it) [Team et al., 2025]. Following the SFT distillation procedure described in Section 2.1, we employ GPT-4.1 as the teacher agent to collect 3,000 trajectories from the training sets of MATH [Hendrycks et al., 2021] and HotpotQA [Yang et al., 2018], respectively, and retain only the successful ones to construct the distillation dataset. Implementation Details. All experiments use the CodeAct framework [Wang et al., 2024], with the web-search tool implemented following [Kang et al., 2025, Jin et al., 2025]. For both SFT and ProD, we train separate LoRA weights [Hu et al., 2022] for each task with rank 64, batch size 32, AdamW, and linear learning rate schedule with 3% warmup. ProD initializes from the SFT-distilled student agent and is further optimized. The main results in Section 4.2 use the lexical stagnation score, single ProD iteration, and an adaptive-margin weighting of α = 0.5. We analyze iterative ProD optimization in Section 4.4, and report results using alternative stagnation scores in Appendix F. During inference, we use greedy decoding and cap the interaction horizon at 10 turns. Additional hyperparameter details (e.g., learning rate, training epochs, c0, and λ) are provided in Appendix B.1. Datasets and Evaluation. We evaluate agentic capabilities primarily through factual and mathematical reasoning tasks, covering code-assisted numerical computation, software execution, and web-based information seeking. We consider both in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD) generalization. For ID evaluation, we use MATH and HotpotQA. We sample 110 problems from each of the seven MATH subjects (770 in total) and 500 hard-level questions from HotpotQA. To assess OOD 6 Figure 3: Alleviating progress stagnation. Comparison between SFT and ProD agents: Columns 1&2 show turn-level lexical stagnation on MATH and HotpotQA, Columns 3&4 show average semantic and judgment stagnation across turns and datasets. generalization, we utilize Omni-MATH [Gao et al., 2025], sampling 500 problems from difficulty levels 13 and another 500 from levels 45. We also include 500 instances from 2WikiMultiHopQA [Ho et al., 2020] to provide broader coverage of web-search-based multi-hop factual reasoning. Following prior work [Kang et al., 2025, Gao et al., 2025], we rely on an LLM-as-Judge (GPT-4.1-mini) to determine accuracy by comparing generated answers with ground-truth reference. Evaluation prompts are provided in Appendix B.2. Additionally, we use stagnation scores and related efficiency metrics to quantify the practical utility of our method in reducing stagnant interaction loops. 4.2 Main Results ProD consistently surpasses SFT distillation in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings. Table 3 reports the accuracy of 8 student agents across multiple benchmarks. Compared with the base models, ProD yields substantial absolute improvements and consistently outperforms standard SFT distillation across all model families. On average, ProD improves in-domain accuracy by 29.2% over base models and by 4.7% over SFT, while achieving out-of-domain gains of 18.5% and 4.9%, respectively. Notably, ProD exhibits average relative improvement of approximately 10% in-domain and 17% out-of-domain over SFT. ProD enables students to narrow the gap to their teacher. For instance, on HotpotQA, the Qwen3-4B student distilled via ProD achieves 70.8% accuracy, nearly matching the teachers performance of 71.0%. ProD also outperforms rejection-sampling SFT, as shown in Appendix L. These results underscore ProDs ability to enhance both the fundamental effectiveness and the generalization of SLM-based agents. Table 4: Inference efficiency averaged over 8 student agents on ID and OOD settings. ProD effectively mitigates progress stagnation and enhances task efficiency. In Figure 3, we compare the stagnation patterns of SFT and ProD agents. The results show that ProD substantially alleviates stagnation across lexical, semantic, and LLMas-judge metrics, allowing student agents to maintain smoother trajectories that align more closely with the teachers behavior. Additional Gemma3 results are provided in Appendix G, and qualitative examples are shown in Appendix P. Beyond trajectory quality, Table 4 reports the average number of interaction turns and token consumption, averaged over eight student agents in both ID and OOD settings. By explicitly penalizing stagnant reasoning-action patterns, ProD enables agents to solve tasks more decisively. This leads to consistent reduction in interaction length across most SLMs on all benchmarks, demonstrating that ProD not only improves accuracy but also significantly enhances overall task efficiency. We compare against two representative methods that suppress redundant generation at the decoding level and at the training-data level, respectively. Specifically, Repetition 7 Figure 4: Iterative ProD further alleviates stagnation (1&2) and improves accuracy (3&4) on MATH. Penalty (RP) [Keskar et al., 2019, vLLM, 2026] operates at decoding time by rescaling the logits of previously generated tokens to discourage excessive repetition. We apply RP on top of SFT-distill with penalty strengths of 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3. The other family reduces redundancy at the data level by shortening teacher demonstrations before distillation. For example, Wu et al. [2025] compress long chain-of-thought traces into concise variants. In the agent-distillation setting, we implement this strategy by identifying training examples whose teacher trajectory contains at least 4 steps and prompting the teacher to re-execute the task with its original trajectory as context, producing shorter and less redundant demonstrations (see Appendix for the detailed prompt). This procedure reduces the average number of steps from 4.98 to 2.65. As shown in Table 5, ProD substantially outperforms both methods, indicating that decoding-level diversity enforcement is insufficient to address trajectorylevel stagnation, while overly large penalties further degrade performance. Data-level shortening reduces redundancy in the teacher demonstrations, but does not impose any constraint on the students own behavior during optimization, yielding only minimal gains over SFT distillation. For the Qwen family, ProD students achieve stagnation scores close to those of the teacher. However, for other model families, such as Llama3.2-3B and Llama3.2-1B on MATH, noticeable gap remains despite improvements over standard SFT. Motivated by this, we study additional ProD iterations by using the first-iteration students as new base models, regenerating trajectories, and recomputing stagnation gaps and adaptive margins for further distillation. Figure 4 (1&2) illustrates the stagnation scores after two ProD iterations. The results indicate that two ProD iterations further reduce stagnation, pushing student behavior closer to the teachers progress dynamics. This refinement also yields consistent gains in final answer accuracy, as shown in Figure 4 (3&4). These results suggest that iterative ProD can further alleviate persistent stagnation and improve performance when single round is insufficient to close the teacherstudent behavioral gap. 4.5 Ablation Studies In this section, we examine the key components of ProD, including the adaptive margin and the SFT loss term. We further analyze the sensitivity of the adaptive margin by varying the relative weighting between the stagnation gap and final answer correctness. The results validate these design choices and indicate that both signals are necessary to capture behavioral discrepancies between the student and teacher. Hyperparameter details for the ablations are provided in Appendix B.1. Ablation of Optimization Components. We evaluate two variants to assess the roles of the adaptive margin and the SFT objective: (1) ProD (w/o SFT + AM) removes the SFT loss from L(θ) and replaces the adaptive margin with fixed constant. This version effectively degenerates to SimPO [Meng et al., 2024], albeit using trajectories produced by the current student agent. (2) ProD (w/o AM) retains the SFT loss but adopts fixed margin. As shown in Figure 5, ProD (w/o SFT + AM) exhibits unstable performance and even underperforms the SFT-distilled baseline on Qwen3-4B and Gemma3-4B-it. This underscores the importance of the SFT loss in anchoring the student to valid 8 Figure 5: Ablation of optimization objective components in ProD with two ablated variants, ProD (w/o SFT + AM) and ProD (w/o AM), where AM denotes the adaptive margin. reasoning paths by maintaining high probability on teacher trajectories. In contrast, ProD (w/o AM) consistently outperforms SFT but remains inferior to the full ProD formulation. This suggests that fixed margin may lead to overcorrection or insufficient optimization for varied trajectory qualities, thereby limiting potential gains. These results indicate that the SFT loss and adaptive margin play complementary roles in stabilizing optimization and bolstering performance. Effect of Adaptive Margin Weighting. The coefficient α in Equation (3) balances the stagnation gap and answer correctness, with α = 0.5 used by default in Table 3. Table 6 reports ProD performance under different α values, where α = 1 uses only the stagnation gap and α = 0 uses only answer correctness. Even with the stagnation gap alone (α = 1), ProD substantially improves over the SFT baseline. However, the best average accuracy is consistently achieved at α = 0.5, indicating that balancing both signals provides more fine-grained estimate of behavioral discrepancies and enables more effective control over optimization strength.

Prior works fine-tune student models on complete teacher-generated reasoning chains [Ho et al., 2023, Shridhar et al., 2023]. To reduce noise from lengthy CoT sequences, several methods extract concise or keypoint-focused rationales via token-weighting modules [Feng et al., 2024], reasoning segmentation [Chen et al., 2025], or redundant-step pruning [Wu et al., 2025, Jiang et al., 2025]. UniCoTT [Zhuang et al., 2025] introduces structural-consistency learning for diverse reasoning patterns, while SCOTT [Wang et al., 2023] uses counterfactual training to improve reasoning faithfulness. Pipis et al. [2025] study looping in single-turn CoT distillation and attribute it to hardness-induced risk aversion, highlighting the need for training-time interventions without developing dedicated mitigation objective. In contrast, we study stagnation in agent distillation, characterize it via the teacherstudent stagnation gap, and propose training-time solution. Agent Distillation. Distilling agentic capabilities enables SLMs to learn tool-augmented reasoning rather than merely memorize facts, as in conventional CoT distillation. As result, distilled SLMs exhibit stronger generalization to novel tasks that require previously unseen knowledge. recent foundational work [Kang et al., 2025] establishes an SFT paradigm on teacher-generated interactive trajectories. By masking environmental observations in the training loss, this approach encourages the student to produce coherent thoughts and actions. While effective, it does not adequately address the severe stagnation exhibited by SLMs in interactions, which our method aims to mitigate.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: This work systematically analyzes key limitation of SFT-based agent distillation: progress stagnation. We find that student agents often become trapped in unproductive, failed strategies, and that this issue worsens with longer interaction horizons and smaller model scales. To address it, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and adaptively penalizes stagnation by measuring behavioral discrepancies against teacher trajectories. Through iterative optimization, ProD gradually closes the gap toward teacher-level dynamics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ProD significantly enhances both the task success rates and execution efficiency of SLMs. Future work could develop more fine-grained progress metrics and more precise methods for localizing stagnant actions, enabling targeted corrective signals during agent distillation.

sections.title: B Additional Experimental Details
sections.content: In this section, we present additional implementation details, along with the hyperparameter selection and evaluation prompts used in our experiments. We implement all agents under the CodeAct framework [Wang et al., 2024] using smolagents [Roucher et al., 2025]. The specific version of the 13 teacher agent is gpt-4.1-2025-04-14. All experiments were conducted on single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80GB) and single NVIDIA H200 GPU (140GB). B.1 Hyperparameters Hyperparameters in SFT Distillation. For SFT-based distillation, we first explore range of learning rates on each task and evaluate model checkpoints from different training epochs on indistribution evaluation sets to identify the optimal configuration. The selected model is then directly evaluated under out-of-distribution settings. Concretely, we consider learning rates from the set {2 104, 2 105}, with batch size of 32, the AdamW optimizer, and linear learning rate schedule with 3% warmup ratio. All models are trained for up to 5 epochs, and checkpoints from each epoch are evaluated. The checkpoint achieving the best accuracy is retained as the final SFT-distilled agent, and all reported results, including stagnation scores, final answer accuracy, and task efficiency, are obtained using these selected models. Across all models and tasks, we find that learning rate of 2 104 consistently yields superior performance, which is consistent with prior settings in Kang et al. [2025]. Regarding the number of training epochs, 3 epochs are sufficient for most models to reach optimal performance across tasks. An exception is observed on the MATH benchmark, where Llama3.1-8B and Llama3.2-3B achieve their best results after 2 epochs, and additional training leads to performance degradation. Hyperparameters in Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD). ProD is applied on top of the SFTdistilled SLMs. We use batch size of 32, the AdamW optimizer, and linear learning rate schedule with 3% warmup ratio, consistent with the SFT stage. We fix the log-likelihood scaling parameter β to 2.5 following [Meng et al., 2024]. For the overall objective L(θ) = LPRO(θ) + λ LSFT(θ), we set the weight of the SFT loss term to λ = 1. Empirically, we observe that λ = 1 preserves high log-probability on teacher trajectories throughout training, and therefore we do not further tune this parameter. For the adaptive margin weighting, we set α = 0.5 by default and analyze its sensitivity in Section 4.5. We select the learning rate from {1 105, 5 106, 1 106} and the initial adaptive margin c0 from {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} based on in-domain evaluation results. To further investigate the impact of different training paradigms on this phenomenon, we conduct additional experiments using full-parameter fine-tuning (FFT) for SFT-based agent distillation. Following Appendix B.1, we train FFT for the same number of epochs as the LoRA setting and tune the learning rate over {2 104, 2 105}, selecting 2 105 based on in-domain evaluation performance. The resulting stagnation scores are reported in Figure 6. We find that FFT-distilled agents still exhibit pronounced progress stagnation, indicating that this failure mode is not alleviated by simply increasing the capacity of parameter updates. Moreover, for the Qwen family, stagnation is sometimes even more severe than under LoRA-based fine-tuning. This suggests that unrestricted parameter updates may amplify imitation bias during the distillation process, thereby exacerbating unproductive agent interaction loops. These findings further underscore the importance of explicitly detecting and penalizing progress stagnation exhibited by the student during optimization, rather than relying solely on imitation-based supervision. 15 Figure 6: Comparison of turn-level lexical stagnation scores on MATH and HotpotQA for the teacher agent (GPT-4.1) and SFT-distilled students (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-1.7B, Llama3.1-8B-Inst, and Llama3.2-3B-Inst) trained with LoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning (FFT).

sections.title: D Evaluation of Progress Stagnation on the Distillation Training Data
sections.content: In Figure 2 and Figure 3, we demonstrate that SLMs distilled via SFT exhibit pronounced progress stagnation on held-out in-domain evaluation sets. Here, we further show that this stagnation phenomenon persists even on the SFT distillation dataset itself. Specifically, we let the distilled student agent generate its own interaction trajectories in response to user queries drawn from the distillation dataset D, and compute the stagnation score at each interaction turn. Figure 7 reports the average stagnation scores aggregated over student-generated trajectories from 1,000 sampled user queries, together with the corresponding trajectories produced by the teacher agent. We observe that the student agent exhibits similarly severe stagnation patterns on the training dataset as those observed on held-out evaluation sets. This consistent behavior indicates that imitation-based SFT alone fails to endow student agents with the teachers ability to avoid stagnation, even on the data used for distillation. These findings further motivate the design of ProD, which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation directly on the SFT distillation dataset, enabling the student agent to progressively approximate the teachers behavior. Figure 7: Comparison of turn-level lexical stagnation scores between the teacher agent (GPT-4.1) and SFT-distilled students on the training dataset.

sections.content: In this section, we analyze the gradient of the progress-aware objective in Equation (1) to understand how the adaptive margin modulates the update strength. Our derivation follows the analytical framework of SimPO [Meng et al., 2024], while introducing trajectory-dependent margin to capture progress signals: θLPRO(θ) = β (x,τ )D, τ pθ0 (x) (cid:104) wθ(τ , τ ) (cid:16) τ θ log pθ S(τ x) 1 τ θ log pθ S(τ x) , (4) (cid:17)(cid:105) where wθ(τ , τ ) = σ (cid:16) β τ log pθ S(τ x) β τ log pθ (cid:17) S(τ x) + (τ , τ ) 16 denotes the gradient weight induced by LPRO. Because the adaptive margin (τ , τ ) in Equation (3) accounts for both the stagnation severity of the student trajectory and the correctness of the final outcome, student trajectories that exhibit stronger stagnation and yield incorrect answers are assigned larger margins, which in turn produce larger gradient weights. Conversely, student trajectories that make progress comparable to the teacher and reach correct final answers receive smaller margins and are thus down-weighted during optimization. Consequently, our instance-dependent margin design, driven by the stagnation gap between student and teacher trajectories, focuses updates on unproductive student behaviors while avoiding unnecessary over-correction on trajectories that already exhibit competent progress.

sections.title: H Training Overhead
sections.content: ProD is applied on top of SFT, with additional cost mainly arising from student rollout generation, stagnation-score computation, and ProD training, where the main experiments use the lexical variant of the stagnation score. Table 10 reports the wall-clock time of each component for two representative models, with all experiments conducted on single H200 GPU. For each training question, only one student rollout is required, which is generated once as preprocessing step rather than within the training loop. For 3,000 student trajectories, rollout generation and stagnation-score computation take approximately 1.48 per trajectory for Qwen3-4B and 0.89 per trajectory for Qwen3-1.7B, with total times of 73.8 and 44.4 minutes, respectively. sections.title: I Additional ProD Iterations
sections.content: To examine whether the gains from iterative ProD continue beyond the two iterations studied in Section 4.4, we extend the experiment to four iterations on Llama3.2-3B for MATH. Table 11 reports task accuracy and the average turn-level lexical stagnation score. Most of the improvement in both metrics is achieved within the first two iterations. Accuracy peaks at the third iteration, while the stagnation score changes little after the second iteration. Performance remains relatively stable with further iterations, with no observed collapse through the fourth iteration, which still substantially outperforms the SFT baseline. Each additional iteration requires regenerating student rollouts and performing another round of training, so the cumulative cost grows approximately linearly with the number of iterations. Given the limited gains beyond the second iteration in this setting, one or two iterations provide favorable balance between training cost and performance. Specifically, for teacher trajectories with at least four interaction steps, we prompt the teacher model to solve the same question again using its original successful trajectory as context. Here, we further compare against on-policy DPO [Rafailov et al., 2023]. ProD differs from SimPO and DPO by using an adaptive margin explicitly defined by the teacherstudent stagnation gap and dynamically adjusted according to trajectory severity. In contrast, SimPO and DPO use fixed-margin or margin-free preference objectives without accounting for trajectory-specific stagnation. As shown in Table 12, both baselines underperform ProD, with DPO falling below SFT on Gemma3-4B. These results demonstrate that the adaptive margin is essential, as non-adaptive preference objectives can either overcorrect or under-optimize trajectories of varying quality. sections.title: P Qualitative Study
sections.content: In this section, we present qualitative analysis of two case studies, each consisting of paired comparison between interaction trajectories of student agents distilled with SFT and ProD, generated on two sampled questions from the HotpotQA evaluation set. Figure 10 uses the same two-hop query as Figure 1. We observe that the SFT-distilled agent initially issues single search query that attempts to cover keywords from both hops simultaneously. When the returned observation does not contain the relevant evidence, the agent continues to persist with highly similar, unsuccessful actions in subsequent turns, failing to acquire new information that would drive progress. In contrast, the ProD-distilled agent follows solution pattern that closely mirrors the teacher trajectory in Figure 1: it executes clear two-hop search procedure and uses intermediate observations to guide subsequent steps, resulting in steady progress toward the answer. Figure 11 exhibits similar failure mode. Although the SFT-distilled agent recognizes that the first-turn search does not yield useful information, it remains trapped in loop of near-duplicate search attempts. By comparison, the ProD-distilled agent, after two unsuccessful trials, shifts its search strategy at the third turn in way that is meaningfully different from the prior failed actions. This change enables the agent to escape the stagnation loop, retrieve the required evidence, and ultimately solve the question. Overall, these examples illustrate that ProD produces student agents with smoother task execution and stronger ability to break out of unproductive interaction loops compared to SFT distillation. Figure 10: Qualitative comparison between SFTand ProD-distilled Qwen3-1.7B student agents on two-hop HotpotQA question. The SFT-distilled agent repeatedly issues similar search queries that attempt to jointly cover both hops, failing to extract useful intermediate information and exhibiting persistent progress stagnation (left). In contrast, the ProD-distilled agent decomposes the task into clear two-hop search process, leveraging intermediate observations to guide subsequent actions and achieving steady progress toward the correct answer (right). 21 Figure 11: Qualitative comparison between SFTand ProD-distilled Qwen3-4B student agents on HotpotQA evaluation example. Although the SFT-distilled agent recognizes the failure of its initial search attempt, it remains trapped in loop of near-duplicate queries without acquiring new information (left). By contrast, the ProD-distilled agent adapts its search strategy after early unsuccessful attempts, escapes the stagnation loop, and successfully retrieves the required information to solve the task (right).

sections.title: Q Discussion
sections.content: Limitations. Our OOD evaluation primarily reflects cross-dataset shifts within the same broad task families. For example, the shift from MATH to Omni-MATH involves moving from high-school competition math to more challenging Olympiad-level problems. Thus, these results should be interpreted as evidence of generalization across datasets within these task families, rather than to entirely new domains. Additionally, stagnation scores should be interpreted as auxiliary diagnostic metrics, while task accuracy remains the primary evaluation metric. Our work focuses on measuring and mitigating stagnation at the trajectory level, where the goal is to quantify how much student trajectory deviates from the teacher in maintaining progress. This design is effective for identifying broad teacherstudent behavioral gaps, but it does not fully explain the root causes of stagnation. For example, student may stagnate because it misinterprets an observation, fails to update its plan, over-trusts failed tool call, or lacks the task knowledge needed to propose new direction. Our current stagnation scores do not explicitly distinguish these cases. Future work could develop more fine-grained progress metrics that localize stagnation to specific reasoning steps, tool calls, or observation updates, and use this diagnosis to provide more targeted corrective signals during training. Broader Impact and Safeguard Statement. This work improves agent distillation by mitigating progress stagnation in SLM agents, enabling more robust and decisive multi-turn task execution. We expect these advances to support more efficient distillation of reliable autonomous agents from stronger teacher models, especially in settings where large proprietary agents are costly to deploy. At the same time, making agentic capabilities available in smaller and locally deployable models raises important safety considerations, since such agents may interact with external tools, execute code, or retrieve information from the web. To reduce these risks, our current implementation uses the CodeAct framework, which executes code in sandboxed environment with restricted tool access, providing basic safety guardrails. However, sandboxing alone is not complete safety solution. When releasing our code and models, we will include usage guidelines and safeguards to discourage misuse.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The limitations are provided in Appendix Q. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not include theoretical results. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have provided detailed experimental settings including hyperparameters needed to reproduce the experimental results in Appendix B. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? 25 Answer: [Yes] Justification: Code, data and instructions for reproducing the experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/CaoYuanpu/ProD. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have provided detailed experimental settings in Section 4 and Appendix B. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: We do not include error bars due to the high computational and evaluation costs involved. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: This is provided in Appendix B. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The research conducted in the paper conforms with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have provided such discussion in Appendix Q. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. 27 The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: We have described safeguards in Appendix Q. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: All the creators and original owners of assets used in the paper are properly credited. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. 28 If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The released code is documented at https://github.com/CaoYuanpu/ ProD, including data access and experimental reproduction instructions. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing experiments or research with human subjects. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing experiments or research with human subjects. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper. We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution. 29 For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review. 16. We provide detailed descriptions of these uses in Appendix B. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the core method development in this research does not involve LLMs as any important, original, or non-standard components. Please refer to our LLM policy in the NeurIPS handbook for what should or should not be described.
